question: Natura 2000 – ‘Gut Walterskirchen’ European protected area

How, in the Commission’s view, it is possible or allowed that Walterskirchen – which has been a nature reserve since 1952 and was declared a European protected area (‘Gut Walterskirchen’) by decree of the Government of the Province of Carinthia of 29 July 2025 – is in fact being massively downsized (according to the ground plan) through the designation of ‘guaranteed areas’?

To what extent does removing the protection by means of Article 45 of the Carinthian Spatial Planning Act 2021 (K-ROG 2021) and the Carinthian Municipality Planning Law conflict with the ‘principle of equality’ (held to be unconstitutional in Austrian Constitutional Court rulings) if this is expected to lead to a deterioration in part of the protected area, and, given the primacy of EU law over national law, is removing the protection permissible at all?

Does the Commission think, given the ‘ban on deterioration’ (i.e. exceeding the permitted use), that the development or expansion of nature conservation areas by means of a new construction should have been permitted at all, and should the construction have been taken down instead?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.2.

2026) While the Commission has no information on the results of a screening or an appropriate assessment under the Habitats Directive1, the management plan of the site2 requires measures to ensure that the ‘guaranteed areas’ do not negatively impact the adjacent protected habitats and species and concludes that the designation of ‘guaranteed areas’ does not adversely affect protected habitats and species.

The Commission has no competence to assess the compatibility of the Carinthian Spatial Planning Act or other related land planning acts with the Austrian Constitution. The Commission notes that the quoted laws do not seem to directly transpose the obligations of the Habitats and Birds3 Directives.

Changes in the land planning acts cannot by themselves cause deteriorations in the sense of Article 6(2) of the Habitats Directive4. It is the obligation of the competent authorities to ensure that subsequent land development activity, based on these land planning acts, does not lead to such a deterioration.

According to Article 6(3) of the Habitats Directive, it is for the national authorities to assess, on a case-by-case basis, whether a project could cause significant negative effects on a Natura 2000 site in view of its conservation objectives, and to authorise it only after having ascertained that it will not adversely affect the integrity of the site.
It is the primary responsibility of the competent Austrian administrative and judicial authorities to ensure full implementation of these provisions.
1 Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and

flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992. 2 Natura 2000-Gebietsmanagementplan Projekt-Nr.: K8245296, Jänner 2025 EZ 01 GUT WALTERSKIRCHEN AT2119000, Bericht (Hauptteil): https://www.ktn.gv.at/DE/repos/files/ktn.gv.at/Abteilungen/Abt8/Dateien/Naturschutz/Managementplaene/AT21 19000_Gut_Walterskirchen/MP_Gut_Walterskirchen_Hauptbericht_2025.pdf?exp=1692915&fps=1983b4760f9 fcfd1b63c2929fca605e1eebea3d0.

3 Directive 2009/147/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on the conservation of wild birds (OJ L 20/7, 26.1.2010) that codifies the Council Directive 79/409/EEC of 2 April 1979 on the conservation of wild birds.

4 Article 6(2) requires Member States to take appropriate steps to ‘avoid, in the special areas of conservation, the deterioration of natural habitats and the habitats of species as well as disturbance of the species for which the areas have been designated, in so far as such disturbance could be significant in relation to the objectives of this Directive’.
